d: Unmarried, of a person not in a state of wedlock, whether he or she has formerly been married or not.

e.t: This word means “unmarried,” referring to a person who does not have a spouse. It describes marital status rather than an action or event. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in 1 Corinthians 7, where Paul uses it when speaking about people who are not married. The word itself identifies their condition; the surrounding verse determines what is said about that condition in each passage.

This word refers to a rooster, the male chicken. It is a straightforward noun naming the bird known for crowing, especially around the dawn. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 12 times across 11 verses, appearing in Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John. Its repeated use in the Gospel accounts reflects ordinary references to a familiar household or village bird, rather than an abstract idea. The word itself names the rooster; the meaning of any particular mention depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

This word means “not salty” or “unsalty,” describing something that lacks saltiness. It functions as a descriptive word for the condition of being without salt, rather than naming salt itself or an action involving salt. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 9:50. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains the absence of saltiness.

This word means “help,” referring to aid given to someone who needs support. It presents helping as a useful contribution, something offered for another person’s benefit. In the Greek New Testament, it appears only once, in 1 Corinthians 12:28. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that verse must be understood from its context, but its central meaning remains help or assistance provided to others.

d: To chatter, to be long-winded, utter empty words, stammer, repeat.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Subjunctive, second, Plural

e.t: This word means “to babble,” describing speech that becomes repetitive, empty, or uncontrolled rather than a clear, purposeful request. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, at Matthew 6:7. That single occurrence establishes its ordinary lexical sense, while the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain exactly how the word functions there. Its focus is on the manner of speaking, not simply on speaking or praying itself.

This word refers to a purpose or resolution—the settled intention or decision behind an action. It can describe what someone plans, determines, or has decided to do. As a noun, it identifies an intended course or considered decision rather than the action itself. The word occurs nine times in the Greek New Testament, including several passages in 1 Corinthians and Revelation. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context, but its central idea remains a purpose or resolution held in mind.

me: Verb, Imperfect, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This word means “to murmur” or “to mutter”—to express dissatisfaction or complaint in a low, grumbling way. It describes spoken grumbling rather than a clear, open declaration. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Luke, so its meaning is focused and consistent within this corpus. The surrounding verse determines who is murmuring and what prompted it, but the word itself points to a dissatisfied response voiced under one’s breath or in complaint.

d: To gird, tie around; to gird round myself.

e.t: This word means “to tie around” or “to wrap around.” It describes the action of putting something around oneself or another person, commonly with a cloth or garment. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in John, describing an action involving something tied or wrapped around the body. Its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding verse and scene, but the central idea remains securing or placing something around someone. This is an action word rather than a name for the object being used.

This word refers to a guarantee or to a guarantor—the person who provides assurance that an obligation will be fulfilled. It can therefore describe either the assurance itself or the one who stands behind it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 7:22. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is dependable security given on behalf of another.

This word means “mercy”: compassionate kindness shown toward someone in need or distress. It describes a quality God shows and a quality people are called to practice. In the New Testament, mercy is treated as weightier than outward religious observance when separated from a genuinely obedient heart. It also appears in praise of God’s continuing compassion and in the call to respond mercifully toward others. This word occurs 27 times in the Greek New Testament, across 26 verses, showing a recurring emphasis on compassionate action and God’s gracious character.

d: The material of a building, a structure.

e.t: This word means “material,” referring to substance used in describing something made or constructed. It is a Greek New Testament word found once, in Revelation 21:18. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, its precise role in that sentence cannot be described further. Its central meaning remains material: something that forms or is used in the composition of a structure or object.

e.t: This word means “to deceive” or describes someone as “deceived.” It refers to misleading a person so that he or she accepts what is false or is turned away from sound judgment. As a verb, it can describe either the act of deceiving or the resulting condition of being deceived. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, showing a recurring concern that people not be led astray by false appearances, persuasive speech, or mistaken understanding.

d: Gentle, mild, forbearing, fair, reasonable, moderate.

e.t: This word means “gentle,” describing a person whose conduct is mild, considerate, and not harsh. In the Greek New Testament, it appears five times, applied to qualities expected in Christian conduct and leadership. Its use in Philippians, 1 Timothy, Titus, James, and 1 Peter shows that gentleness is treated as a recognizable character quality across different instructions and settings. The word does not describe weakness; it identifies a manner that is restrained and gracious rather than severe. Its precise emphasis in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

d: To fear, to be anxious, to be cautious; to reverence.
me: Verb, Aorist, passive depOnent, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word describes having holy fear and showing reverence. It refers to an attitude of serious respect toward God, not merely ordinary fright. As a verb, it expresses the response of treating God as worthy of honor and careful obedience. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 11:7. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on reverent fear before God.

d: To lay hold of, fasten on to, seize, attack.
me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Indicative, third, Singular

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to attach” or “to fasten.” It describes securing one thing to another so that it is held in place. The meaning points to a concrete joining or securing action rather than a general feeling or idea. This word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 28:3. The surrounding verse is needed to explain what was attached and why, but the word itself supplies the basic sense of fastening something in place.

d: Cappadocia, a large Roman province in the central eastern part of Asia Minor.

e.t: Cappadocia is the name of a region mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It identifies a place rather than describing an action, quality, or person. The word appears twice in this corpus, in Acts 2:9 and 1 Peter 1:1, and both occurrences are rendered “Cappadocia.” Its basic meaning is therefore a geographical name that locates people or groups connected with that region.

d: To understand, take in a fact about, consider carefully.
me: Verb, second Aorist, Active, iMperative, second, Plural

e.t: This word means “notice carefully” or “to consider.” It calls for focused attention rather than a quick glance, urging someone to observe something closely and think about what it reveals. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Matthew 6:28, and is rendered “Consider.” Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself expresses deliberate observation and thoughtful attention.

d: A word of command, a call, an arousing outcry.

e.t: This word means a command: an authoritative call or order given to direct someone’s action. It names the command itself rather than describing the person who gives it or the response that follows. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Thessalonians 4:16. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how that command functions in that passage, but the word’s basic sense remains a directive issued with authority.

This Greek New Testament word can refer to a “bedroom” or to a “chamberlain.” It therefore names either a private room or a person identified with that household role, depending on how it is used. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 12:20. Its precise sense in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its translation, but these are the two recorded lexical meanings.

me: Verb, Present, Middle, Subjunctive, third, Singular

e.t: This word means “to grow,” describing increase or development. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Mark 4:27, so its normal meaning is supported by a single occurrence rather than a broad range of passages. The word itself expresses the process of becoming larger, more developed, or more mature; the surrounding verse determines what is growing in that particular setting.

d: Miletus, a city on the coast of the Roman province Asia.

e.t: Miletus is the name of a place mentioned in the Greek New Testament. It functions as a proper name rather than a description of a person, action, or quality. The word occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, appearing twice in Acts and once in 2 Timothy. In each recorded occurrence, it is rendered “Miletus,” preserving the place name rather than translating it into another descriptive term.

d: To be short-sighted, blink, see dimly.

e.t: This word means “be nearsighted”: it describes someone whose vision is limited so that nearby things are clearer than distant things. It is a descriptive verb, focusing on the condition of having restricted sight rather than naming a person or object. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 1:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the basic word picture is limited vision and difficulty seeing clearly.

In the Greek New Testament, this word means “likeness” or “similarity”—a resemblance between one thing and another. It describes correspondence in some respect without saying that the two things are identical in every way. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, both times in Hebrews, so its meaning is focused rather than broad across the corpus. It appears in Hebrews 4:15 and 7:15; the surrounding verse text is needed to explain the specific comparison in each passage.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “from childhood.” It describes something that has been true or experienced since a person’s earliest years, marking the starting point in childhood rather than a later beginning. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Mark 9:21. Its basic sense identifies how long something has been present, while the surrounding verse determines what specific condition or circumstance is being described.

e.t: This word means “to set before”: to place something in front of someone or present it for attention or use. It is a verb describing an action, not merely the object being placed. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 19 times in 18 verses, including scenes involving food being placed before people and the presentation of something for consideration. The surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis is on physically setting something down or presenting it more broadly, but the central idea remains placing something before others.

This word means “flock,” referring to a group of sheep gathered together and cared for as a unit. It is a noun used for an actual flock, including one watched by shepherds or belonging to someone who tends animals. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, consistently carrying this concrete sense. Its wider significance in any particular passage comes from the surrounding words and subject, but the word itself names the flock rather than the shepherd or the act of caring for it.

e.t: This word means “to approach” or “to come to,” describing movement toward someone or something. It is an action word that focuses on drawing near rather than simply being present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 10:35. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is the act of coming near or approaching.

This word refers to a bier or coffin—a container used to carry or hold a dead person. It is a noun describing the physical object itself, not the person who has died or the act of burial. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 7:14. Its meaning is therefore specific and concrete: a bier or coffin mentioned in that passage. The surrounding verse supplies the particular significance of the object there.

This word means “sponge,” referring to an absorbent object used to hold or apply liquid. It occurs three times in the Greek New Testament, in Matthew, Mark, and John. Each occurrence uses the same ordinary noun, so its basic meaning is straightforward rather than symbolic or abstract. The word identifies a physical object, while the surrounding verse determines how it is being used in that particular scene.

d: Stephen, one of the seven original deacons at Jerusalem, and the first martyr.

e.t: Stephen is a personal name referring to the man called Stephen in the book of Acts. As a name, it identifies a particular person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. The Greek New Testament uses this name six times, all in Acts, from Acts 6:5 through Acts 22:20. Those occurrences consistently render the name as “Stephen.” Understanding the word therefore depends less on translating a general concept and more on recognizing whom the name identifies in the surrounding passage.

This Greek New Testament word means “sympathetic”: responsive to another person’s suffering or circumstances with fellow-feeling and concern. It describes an attitude toward others rather than an action or object. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Peter 3:8, so its meaning is represented by a single occurrence in that corpus. Its central idea is sharing another person’s experience emotionally enough to respond with understanding and care.

d: To dare, endure, to be bold, have courage, make up the mind.

e.t: This word means to dare, be bold, or show courage to do something. It describes a person taking action despite difficulty, risk, opposition, or the possibility of rejection. In the Greek New Testament, it can express the willingness to approach, speak, or act boldly. The word occurs 16 times across 15 New Testament verses, so its exact force depends on the sentence: it may describe courageous action or the boldness needed to attempt something. Its core idea is courage expressed through deliberate action.

This Greek New Testament word can mean “course” or “wheel,” naming a course or a wheel according to the sentence in which it appears. Its central idea is a course as a path, or a wheel as a round object associated with movement. It occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in James 3:6; the surrounding verse text is needed to determine which sense is intended there.

This word refers to a female pig, specifically a sow. It is a concrete noun naming the animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:22. Its ordinary meaning is clear from the word’s direct gloss, while its precise force in that passage belongs to the surrounding context. No broader meaning should be added beyond what the context supports.

“Gossipy” describes speech or conduct centered on sharing personal matters about other people, especially in an idle or intrusive way. The word identifies a negative kind of talk rather than a useful report or careful communication. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Timothy 5:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning points to gossiping behavior or speech.

e.t: This word describes being “on the ground” or moving “to the ground.” It points to the ground as a person’s or object’s location or destination, rather than naming the ground itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, both in John: once in John 9:6 and again in John 18:6. Its exact force in either verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains a position or movement involving the ground.

This word means “written code”. It refers to something formally set down in writing rather than spoken or merely remembered. As a noun, it names the written statement itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Colossians 2:14. That reference identifies its only occurrence, while the surrounding verse is needed to explain how the word functions there. Its central idea remains a written code or written statement.

d: The skin, surface of the body.

e.t: This word means “skin,” referring to the outer covering of a person’s body. It names the bodily surface itself rather than an inward feeling, condition, or spiritual quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 19:12. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise role in that sentence must be understood from the context of that passage. Its basic meaning remains straightforward: the physical skin covering the body.

This word means “fog” or “mist”: a cloudlike veil of fine moisture that makes the air hazy and obscures clear sight. It is a concrete word for a temporary atmospheric covering, not a person, action, or moral quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Peter 2:17. The precise force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a fog or mist.
